tldr: Without any drift references or drift-related rewards, this paper shows that simply minimizing lap times through learning control naturally causes drift to emerge from grip driving on low-friction surfaces as tires approach their handling limit.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed BE-LMPC. By updating an empirical safe set across laps and expanding the exploration boundary, it enables a continuous transition (emergence) from grip driving to drift when performance demands reach the tire's capacity.
overview:
In autonomous vehicle drift control, the dominant approach has been to prescribe a steady-state drift equilibrium, sideslip reference, or trajectory, and then track it. However, this prescribe-and-track formulation cannot explain the fundamental mechanism of why and how a vehicle transitions from everyday grip driving into drift as a natural outcome of pursuing speed.

To tackle this, the authors asked: "Can drift emerge autonomously when lap time minimization is the only objective, without any explicit drift command?" By analyzing the mathematical properties of vehicle dynamics and tire models, they formulated the transition from tire adhesion to sliding as a state-space continuous process, and characterized drift as a "conditional emergence phenomenon" that occurs only when the ratio of performance demand to available tire capacity reaches its limit.

To observe this phenomenon, they developed Boundary Exploration Learning Model Predictive Control (BE-LMPC), an extension of Learning Model Predictive Control (LMPC). It builds an empirical safe set and a terminal cost from completed laps that stayed within track boundaries, progressively widening the allowable sideslip and yaw rate boundaries while ensuring recoverability. Crucially, the controller's objective function contains no drift-encouraging terms whatsoever.

Simulations on a track with tire-road friction coefficient $\mu=0.6$ revealed that as lap times improved over repeated runs, sustained drift with high sideslip angles and rear-axle saturation suddenly emerged on Lap 11. Conversely, on high-friction surfaces ($\mu=0.8\sim 1.2$), no drift occurred even when reaching similar peak speeds. This demonstrates that drift is not a separately engineered motion mode, but a physically inevitable continuation of limit handling.
contributions: Formulating and demonstrating for the first time the autonomous transition (emergence) from grip driving to drift in a repetitive lap time minimization task without any drift commands or rewards.

Mechanically proving, via models such as the Fiala tire model, that the transition from tire adhesion to sliding is state-space continuous (Lipschitz continuous), meaning drift is a continuous response within the same underlying dynamics.
Designing BE-LMPC, a learning MPC that safely unlocks limit handling behaviors by progressively expanding exploration boundaries gated by safe recoverability.

Clarifying through friction sweeps and sensitivity analyses that drift emergence is not a matter of speed alone, but a conditional phenomenon governed by the ratio between performance demand and tire friction capacity.

sections.heading: Drift: From Something Prescribed to Something That Naturally Emerges
sections.summary: Existing autonomous drift studies focus on tracking target trajectories or equilibria, leaving the continuous transition from normal driving to high-sideslip motion unexplained. This paper tests whether drift autonomously emerges under identical vehicle models and controllers by purely pursuing lap time minimization.
sections.details:
Drifting is a limit-handling motion where the rear wheels approach friction saturation and the vehicle body operates at a large sideslip angle (the misalignment between heading and travel direction). To date, autonomous driving research has primarily relied on drift equilibrium points and nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) to track and stabilize explicitly prescribed drift states.

However, this "prescribe-and-track" paradigm cannot explain why the dynamics naturally transition from grip driving into limit handling. When a race car driver drifts while shaving lap times, that motion is not an externally instructed mode; it is a natural physical response at the tire limit.

This study explores whether a continuous transition from grip driving to sustained drift can be observed during iterative learning in a lap-minimization task without any drift references. The key is to capture this phenomenon within a single, completely unchanged closed-loop system, without switching vehicle models or controllers.

sections.heading: Capturing Tire Limit Continuity with Combined-Slip Dynamics
sections.summary: The study adopts a planar 3-DOF single-track (bicycle) model paired with a combined-slip Fiala tire model that accounts for friction coupling between longitudinal and lateral directions. Front-to-rear drive distribution is fixed at 50:50, and the exact same nonlinear model is shared between the controller and the plant to isolate the core emergence mechanism.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Vehicle Configuration and State Equations
The analysis uses a planar 3-DOF single-track (bicycle) model tracking velocity $v$, vehicle sideslip angle $\beta$, yaw rate $r$, and planar coordinates. It relies solely on front-wheel steering $\delta$, excluding complex actuation schemes like rear-wheel steering or direct yaw moment control.

### 2.2 Drive Force Control and Longitudinal Distribution
Drive force is abstracted into wheel forces based on throttle and braking commands, factoring in power limits and rolling resistance. The front-to-rear drive force distribution ratio is strictly fixed at $\lambda_x = 0.5$ (50:50). While normal tire loads $F_{zi}$ shift dynamically due to quasi-static longitudinal load transfer, there are no drive-torque-vectoring tricks used to artificially induce drift.

### 2.3 Combined-Slip Tire Model
The Fiala tire model is employed. By incorporating friction circle constraints, the model captures combined-slip characteristics where generating longitudinal force $F_{xi}$ reduces the available lateral friction capacity $\bar{\mu}_i F_{zi}$. This accurately represents handling limits during simultaneous cornering and acceleration or braking. Furthermore, the exact same mathematical formulation is shared between the simulation plant and the internal controller model, ensuring that the findings highlight pure learning dynamics rather than plant-model mismatch.

captions.F1: The planar 3-DOF single-track (bicycle) model, defining the geometric relationships among CG velocity $v$, vehicle sideslip angle $\beta$, yaw rate $r$, front steering angle $\delta$, and longitudinal/lateral forces.

sections.heading: What is Drift "Emergence"? Proving a Mathematically Continuous Transition
sections.summary: The paper provides an objective operational definition of drift emergence (large sideslip, high yaw rate, rear-axle saturation, and sustained duration). It also proves that the transition from tire adhesion to sliding forms a continuous (Lipschitz continuous) vector field, arguing that drift boundary reachability is governed by the ratio of required performance to friction capacity.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Operational Definition of Drift Emergence
The paper defines drift emergence as the autonomous formation of sustained, high-sideslip cornering as performance improves, without any drift reference or reward in the controller objective. Drift is formally detected when three conditions are simultaneously met: sideslip angle $|\beta| \ge 8^\circ$, yaw rate $|r| \ge 0.45\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, and rear axle utilization $\rho_r \ge 0.82$, sustained for at least $T_{\rm d} = 0.30\,\mathrm{s}$ (6 control steps). A brief rear-end slide is not classified as drift.

### 3.2 Continuity Between Grip and Drift
While "grip driving" and "drifting" appear to be distinct motion modes, there is no discontinuous jump in the underlying dynamic equations. The paper shows that under locally Lipschitz continuous tire characteristics, the vehicle state vector field is continuous, yielding continuous trajectory solutions. In the combined-slip Fiala model, lateral force and its derivative (cornering power) smoothly approach zero at the boundary between adhesion and sliding, preserving $C^1$ continuity.

### 3.3 Conditionality of Drift Emergence (Boundary Reachability)
Continuity does not imply that drift will appear in every scenario simply by lowering lap times. The authors define the "boundary reachability ratio" $\mathcal{R} = v_{\rm att} / v_{\rm grip}$, which compares the centripetal acceleration demanded by track curvature $\kappa$ and speed against the grip limit speed $v_{\rm grip}$ determined by road friction $\mu$. When $\mathcal{R} \ll 1$, the task is easily solved purely with grip. Only when low friction pushes $\mathcal{R} \to 1$ does the drift domain become explorable and advantageous for shaving lap time.

sections.heading: BE-LMPC: Balancing Lap Time Reduction and Safe Boundary Expansion
sections.summary: BE-LMPC builds an empirical safe set and local terminal cost from completed lap data, progressively expanding sideslip and yaw rate exploration boundaries whenever a lap is successfully completed (recoverable). The global speed bound remains fixed, and the controller contains no drift-encouraging terms.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Iterative Tasks and the Empirical Safe Set
The controller builds upon Learning Model Predictive Control (LMPC), which improves performance lap by lap. State samples are gathered from completed laps. To reduce online computation, a local empirical safe set $\mathcal{CS}_t$ is formed via convex combinations of the 16 nearest samples from the two most recent accepted laps. The terminal cost is assigned a remaining step-cost that decreases toward the lap finish line, providing a forward-driving pressure.

### 4.2 Boundary Exploration and Lap Acceptance Criteria
Expanding the exploration envelope all at once risks spin-outs and track boundary violations. To prevent this, a boundary level parameter $\eta_j \in [0, 1]$ gradually loosens the allowable limits on sideslip and yaw rate by $\Delta\eta = 0.2$ per successful lap. Crucially, the global speed limit $v_{\max} = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ remains strictly fixed from start to finish. A completed lap is "accepted" and allowed to advance the exploration boundary only if it stays within track borders and satisfies criteria for solver failure rates and peak tire utilization.

### 4.3 Online Optimization
At each control step ($0.05\,\mathrm{s}$ interval), the system is linearized in a linear time-varying (LTV) fashion around the previous solution and solved as a Quadratic Program (QP). The objective function consists solely of track centerline deviation penalties, acceleration/steering rate smoothing penalties, and terminal progress cost. It contains no target values for $\beta$ or $r$, no countersteering guidance, and no reward for tire slip. Drift emergence is entirely left to the interaction between vehicle dynamics, constraint relaxation, and lap time pressure.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup: Friction Sweeps and Ablation baselines
sections.summary: On an approximately 80.5 m closed track, the authors evaluated friction sweeps from low ($\mu=0.6$) to high ($\mu=1.2$), detector threshold sensitivity analyses, and baseline comparisons against grip-constrained methods.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Track, Vehicle, and Numerical Settings
The testing circuit is a closed loop of length $80.48\,\mathrm{m}$ with a track half-width of $\pm 0.75\,\mathrm{m}$. The first two laps are driven safely at a low speed of $1.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to provide initial data, followed by 10 learning laps from Lap 3 to Lap 12. Plant numerical integration uses a 4th-order Runge-Kutta scheme with a step size of $0.005\,\mathrm{s}$.

### 5.2 Simulation Test Matrix
The evaluation includes:
- **Friction Coefficient Sweep**: Running identical BE-LMPC setups on surfaces with $\mu = 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2$ to examine whether drift occurs.
- **Detector Sensitivity Analysis**: Re-evaluating the $\mu=0.6$ logs offline across modified detection thresholds ($\beta_{\rm th}, \rho_{\rm th}, T_{\rm d}$) to verify that conclusions do not depend on arbitrary detection parameters.
- **Baseline Comparisons**: Benchmarking against a "grip-constrained" method (sideslip restricted to $\le 7^\circ$) and a "fixed-boundary" method (exploration envelope kept at initial levels) to assess differences in lap time and handling behavior.

### 5.3 Evaluation Metrics
Performance is evaluated using lap time, peak/RMS sideslip angle, peak rear axle utilization, drift duration, and track boundary margins. The simulations are deterministic and perfectly matched (no model mismatch), specifically designed to verify the self-consistency of the physical emergence mechanism.

sections.heading: Drift Emerges on Lap 11! The Physics Linking Lap Time and Friction
sections.summary: On the low-friction track ($\mu=0.6$), lap time dropped from 49.95 s to 25.50 s, with drift autonomously emerging on Lap 11. In contrast, on higher friction tracks ($\mu=0.8\sim 1.2$), no drift occurred despite reaching identical peak speeds, proving that drift emerges when performance demand presses against tire capacity.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Drift Emergence Process in Low Friction
At $\mu=0.6$, learning progressed from a Lap 3 time of $49.95\,\mathrm{s}$ (peak $\beta = 5.1^\circ$) until the exploration parameter $\eta$ reached its maximum of 1.0 (fully open) on Lap 8. Drift did not occur immediately upon boundary relaxation; it emerged only on Lap 11 ($26.15\,\mathrm{s}$) as lap time dropped further. It produced a peak sideslip of $14.6^\circ$, rear axle utilization of 0.859, and sustained drift for $0.70\,\mathrm{s}$. By Lap 12, lap time reached $25.50\,\mathrm{s}$, with peak $\beta = 16.5^\circ$ and rear utilization of 0.894. This clearly decouples boundary permissibility from the actual behavioral selection (emergence).

### 6.2 State and Control Comparison Before and After Emergence
Comparing the last pure grip run (Lap 10) with the first drift run (Lap 11), peak speeds were nearly identical: $2.80\,\mathrm{m/s}$ versus $2.88\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (a difference of just $0.08\,\mathrm{m/s}$). Steering inputs remained within roughly the same $\pm 18^\circ$ envelope. Drift was not triggered by higher peak speed or sudden input jumps, but by refined coordination between corner-entry deceleration, attitude adjustment, and corner-exit acceleration, producing nonlinear attitude changes with high sideslip and yaw rates.

### 6.3 Sensitivity Analysis of Detection Criteria
Varying the sideslip threshold from $6^\circ$ to $12^\circ$ did not alter the first detection lap; drift still first appeared on Lap 11. Relaxing the duration threshold $T_{\rm d}$ to $0.20\,\mathrm{s}$ detected drift on Lap 10, while tightening it to $0.50\,\mathrm{s}$ shifted detection to Lap 12. Across all settings, the underlying continuous transition into the high-sideslip regime remained intact.

### 6.4 Friction Sweeps and Baseline Comparison
For $\mu=0.8, 1.0, 1.2$, peak vehicle speeds matched or exceeded the low-friction run (around $2.96\,\mathrm{m/s}$) and lap times reached $25.10\sim 25.50\,\mathrm{s}$, yet zero drift was detected across all laps. On the final lap of $\mu=1.2$, rear axle utilization was merely 0.483; there was simply no physical necessity to slide the tires.
Furthermore, compared to the grip-constrained baseline ($26.70\,\mathrm{s}$) and the fixed-boundary baseline ($26.75\,\mathrm{s}$), BE-LMPC with drift unlocked delivered roughly 4.5% to 4.7% faster lap times, confirming that utilizing the limit-handling envelope directly contributes to performance.

captions.F4: Evolution of drift emergence on road friction $\mu=0.6$: (a) Lap time reduction and exploration boundary level $\eta$ across laps, (b) Trajectory comparison between Lap 10 (grip) and Lap 11 (first drift), and (c) Sideslip ratio and rear axle utilization crossing drift thresholds as laps progress.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: This study demonstrates from both theoretical mechanics and simulation perspectives that pursuing lap time minimization near tire handling limits autonomously produces drift without any drift-specific commands. Future directions include extensions to four-wheel models and real-world experiments.
sections.details:
This paper recharacterizes the transition from grip driving to limit drift as a single, continuous dynamical process without artificial mode switches. It reveals that drift autonomously emerges when performance demands press against tire friction limits, guided safely by boundary exploration learning MPC (BE-LMPC).

Future work includes expanding the plant to a full four-wheel model incorporating lateral load transfer, suspension roll, and wheel rotational/driveline dynamics; adapting to operating environments with time-varying road friction coefficients; and validating the emergence behavior on scaled or full-scale physical vehicle platforms.

takeaways: Drift naturally emerges from unified physical laws when lap time pressure collides with tire friction limits, requiring no dedicated control modes or drift references.
The transition from tire adhesion to sliding is Lipschitz continuous in tire models, confirming drift is a physically smooth continuation of grip driving.
In learning MPC, progressively widening exploration boundaries conditioned on safe recoverability (successfully completed laps) unlocks unstable limit behaviors safely.
The absence of drift on high-friction surfaces is not a failure of control, but because abundant tire capacity removes any physical need to drift ($\mathcal{R} \ll 1$).
limitations: The plant and controller use the exact same planar single-track Fiala model, omitting real-world factors such as lateral load transfer, chassis roll, tire temperature variations, driveline lag, and plant-model mismatch.
The front-to-rear drive distribution is fixed at 50:50, leaving the impact of active drive allocation like torque vectoring on drift emergence unexplored.
Because the controller relies on locally linearized QPs and soft-constrained empirical safe sets, formal control invariance and absolute safety guarantees are not mathematically proven.
